name: Tepetotutla Chinantec
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Tepetotutla Chinantec (tepe1279) is not in the catalog. The single stress-titled item, Westley 1971 'The Tepetotutla Chinantec stressed syllable' (IJAL 37(3):160-163, doi 10.1086/465156), remains paywalled: Crossref/Unpaywall/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar all closed, publisher 403, JSTOR login-gated, no HathiTrust v.37, archive.org has only the 1971 table of contents (which lists the article; saved as receipt). The best first-hand statement available is the author's own summary of that paper in Westley 1991 Tepetotutla Chinantec syntax ch.1 p.1 (SIL PDF via Wayback, already on file; sec.1.6 p.6 adds a ballistic vs controlled stress-type contrast on the stressed syllable. Reading: fixed final word stress. Priority high for acquiring Westley 1971 itself (library/JSTOR), though Westley 1991 already gives the placement rule first-hand. New probe receipts appended to

earlier_scan.source_named: Westley, David. 1971. The Tepetotutla Chinantec Stressed Syllable. IJAL 37(3):160-163. Directly on stress; JSTOR-paywalled, SIL mirrors 403.

new_statements.quote: This chapter is a summary of Westley 1971, where the phonological word was defined as having from one to four syllables, the last of which receives word-level stress (here unmarked). [...] Chinantec roots are almost exclusively monosyllabic; and, due to a very limited system of segmentable forms of inflection, even entire grammatical words are frequently monosyllabic. There are, nevertheless, a few affixes and proclitic grammatical words which may occur in pretonic positions with some word classes, notably verbs, and certain nouns do also occur with pretonic classifiers or participate in compounding of a sort which results in loss of stress of the first of two syllables.
new_statements.citation: Westley, David O. 1991. Tepetotutla Chinantec syntax (Studies in Chinantec Languages 5; SIL & University of Texas at Arlington Publications in Linguistics 106). Dallas: Summer Institute of Linguistics and the University of Texas at Arlington.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 1 'Tepetotutla Chinantec Phonology', p.1 (PDF p.17); supporting: sec.1.6 'Stress' p.6 (PDF p.22) and sec.8.1 p.95 (PDF p.111). scanned text in and; p.1 verified against the page image.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The phonological word consists of one to four syllables and word stress falls on the final syllable (the root/stem syllable); any preceding syllables (inflectional prefixes, proclitics, classifiers, first members of compounds) are pretonic and unstressed. The stressed syllable additionally carries one of two contrastive stress types, ballistic (marked with acute) or controlled (sec.1.6), and its own tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; pretonic syllables are simply 'unstressed' with a reduced (three-way) tone contrast (p.95).
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds 'in which the first element is not reduced phonologically to a pretonic syllable' keep stress on the first element as a separate word (ch.4); footnote 2 p.7 (editor) suggests morphologically complex tone downglides might be reanalysed as stressed syllable + phonologically reduced postposed pronoun; postnuclear person-marking glides /i g/ are part of the stressed syllable, not extra syllables (p.5). Ballistic vs controlled is a contrast of stress TYPE on the stressed syllable, not of position.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word as defined in Westley 1971 (root plus pretonic affixes/proclitics); stress marks are omitted in the 1991 transcription because position is predictable (final). Examples (1) p.1: monosyllable 'soft', disyllable 'monkey', trisyllable 'they have come', four syllables 's/he/they did not conform'.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes the Chinantec of Santa Cruz Tepetotutla, Oaxaca (Westley's fieldwork; principal language consultant Leoncio Hernandez O.), i.e. exactly Glottolog tepe1279 / ISO cnt. Westley 1991 ch.1 is the author's own summary of his 1971 IJAL analysis, so the statement is first-hand though the fuller argument is in the 1971 paper.

new_statements.quote: This chapter is a summary of Westley 1971, where the phonological word was defined as having from one to four syllables, the last of which receives word-level stress (here unmarked). [...] certain nouns do also occur with pretonic classifiers or participate in compounding of a sort which results in loss of stress of the first of two syllables. Pretonic, unstressed syllables have the same general phonological structure as stressed syllables (p.1) [...] 1.6. Stress. Tepetotutla Chinantec has two types of word stress, BALLISTIC and CONTROLLED. [...] a ballistically-stressed syllable (marked by an acute accent /'/) is characterized by a sharp burst of energy at the beginning of the syllable (p.6)
new_statements.citation: Westley, David O. 1991. Tepetotutla Chinantec syntax (Studies in Chinantec Languages 5; SIL and University of Texas at Arlington Publications in Linguistics 106). Dallas: SIL / UT Arlington. Chapter 1 'Tepetotutla Chinantec Phonology', p.1 (PDF p.17) and sec.1.6 'Stress', p.6 (PDF p.22). SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 8916.
new_statements.locator: ch.1, p.1 (opening paragraph) and sec.1.6 Stress, p.6
new_statements.reading: Fixed final word stress: the phonological word has one to four syllables and word-level stress falls on the last syllable; all preceding syllables are pretonic/unstressed (roots are almost all monosyllabic, so most words are one stressed syllable; compounding de-stresses the first of two syllables). Independently of placement, the stressed syllable carries a contrastive ballistic vs controlled stress type (a syllable-type/phonation contrast, not a placement contrast). The author explicitly presents this as a summary of Westley 1971, the Glottolog-listed paper, so it is a first-hand author statement of that paper's analysis.

sources.note: Ch.1 'Tepetotutla Chinantec Phonology' p.1: phonological word has one to four syllables, the LAST of which receives word-level stress; pretonic syllables (a few affixes, proclitics, classifiers, first members of compounds) are unstressed and show fewer contrasts. Sec.1.6 'Stress' p.6: two types of word stress on the stressed syllable, ballistic (acute accent) vs controlled. Sec.1.7 p.7: tone per syllable (H, M, L + two-tone glides). Sec.8.1 p.95: a sentence may begin with an unstressed, ballistically stressed or controlled-stress syllable; 3-way tone contrast on pretonic (unstressed) syllable…

sources.note: Second-hand: several Chinantecan languages 'possess either ballistic stress or controlled stress on stem syllables. In Palantla, Tepetotutla, Sochiapan, and Comaltepec, ballistic syllables have been characterized by an initial surge and rapid decay of intensity...'. No explicit statement of stress position for Tepetotutla beyond 'stem syllables'.
